item.title: What Makes Up the Cosmos? A 20-Year Survey Hints That Something Is Missing.
item.dc:creator: Charlie Wood
item.description:
An era-defining galaxy survey has released its final results. They don’t quite fit the leading theory of cosmology.

The post What Makes Up the Cosmos? A 20-Year Survey Hints That Something Is Missing. first appeared on Quanta Magazine
item.content:encoded:
Joshua Frieman remembers when the world found out that the universe was made of much more than just matter. For a few years, the scientist had been studying the possibility that the cosmos needed something else — a “missing energy” — to make sense. But it was a niche idea. item.title: Can Network Science Transform Health and Nutrition?
item.dc:creator: Steven Strogatz and Janna Levin
item.description:
Albert-László Barabási explains how the same organizing principles shape everything from the internet to the cell, and how mapping the networks inside our bodies could change how we treat disease and think about food.

The post Can Network Science Transform Health and Nutrition? first appeared on Quanta Magazine
item.content:encoded:
Nothing really exists in isolation. Almost every part of our lives exists in a network. Consciousness arises from what neurons do together, life from what genes and proteins do together, society from what we do together. When researchers began mapping real-world networks in the 1990s – from the World Wide Web to Hollywood actors linked by films – they found that wildly different systems shared…

item.title: The Evolving Story of How Chemistry Became Biology
item.dc:creator: Yasemin Saplakoglu
item.description:
After decades of bickering about which molecules came first, a new generation of scientists is rethinking what life was, is, and could be.

The post The Evolving Story of How Chemistry Became Biology first appeared on Quanta Magazine
item.content:encoded:
Around 4.6 billion years ago, some 9 billion years after the birth of the universe, a cloud of gas and dust collapsed into the familiar blinding ball in our sky. Scraps of leftover material collided and accreted into the planets of the solar system, including our own. item.title: How a Metabolic Spark Could Have Jump-Started Life
item.dc:creator: Jake Buehler
item.description:
Energetic pathways that make and break complex molecules are critical to all life. It’s even possible that these self-sustaining cycles could have been key at life’s beginning.

The post How a Metabolic Spark Could Have Jump-Started Life first appeared on Quanta Magazine
item.content:encoded:
For well over 4 billion years, the fire of metabolism has powered the engines of life. The ability of cells to gather, transform, and harness chemical energy from their surroundings is the central force driving the dizzyingly complex network of chemical reactions that sustains living things.
